Iran at War, Canvas Calendar Events

BeCurrent · 8 topics · paste-ready

How to paste one of these

  1. Canvas Calendar, click the day, Edit, then More Options.
  2. Title the event exactly as given on the topic below.
  3. In the Rich Content Editor, click the </> icon to open the HTML editor. Never paste into the visual editor. Pasting rendered HTML there injects wrapper <div>s and inline font declarations that collapse the table.
  4. Press Copy the HTML below, then paste into that HTML editor.
  5. Switch back to the visual editor, delete the [INSERT ASSIGNMENT LINK] placeholder, and insert the real assignment from the right-hand course-links panel, Assignments, click the assignment. Do not hand-type that link; see Section 5 of CANVAS-BUILD-GUIDE.md for why.
  6. Save.

This file is generated

OVERVIEW, LEARNING TARGETS and SUCCESS CRITERIA are lifted verbatim from scripts/lib/unit-content/iran.js. Edit a target there and rerun node scripts/build-canvas-events.js. Never edit a target in Canvas, and never in this file: both are copies, and nothing can tell you when a copy has gone stale.

The markdown twin is docs/canvas/iran-calendar-events.md. It carries the same tables, built by the same function, so the two cannot disagree.

CE - IR1 - The War They Are Watching

Current anchor · 2026

Event title
CE - IR1 - The War They Are Watching
Assignment to link
IR1 - The War They Are Watching · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Establish what is happening now, locate the pressure points, and separate the immediate trigger from the deeper conditions students will test across the unit.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain how Iran, Israel, U.S. regional positions, and the Strait of Hormuz shape the conflict.
  2. I can separate a verifiable event from a claim about why a government acted.
  3. I can propose a starting explanation and identify what evidence could change it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can connect one location to a specific military, economic, or diplomatic consequence.
  2. I can name one verified fact, one interpretation, and one unanswered historical question.
  3. I can rank up to three possible causes and explain why one currently deserves the most weight.

Topic 2

CE - IR2 - The Coup

Reverse History stop · 1951–1953

Event title
CE - IR2 - The Coup
Assignment to link
IR2 - The 1953 Coup · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Examine oil nationalization, the political crisis around Mohammad Mosaddegh, documented U.S. and British covert involvement, and the event's long afterlife in Iranian political memory.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can use a declassified record to establish U.S. involvement without claiming the document proves everything about the coup.
  2. I can explain how oil, sovereignty, domestic politics, and Cold War fears interacted.
  3. I can identify a decision that could plausibly have gone another way and explain why that matters.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can state one claim the archive supports and one claim it cannot establish by itself.
  2. I can connect the 1953 intervention to later distrust through a clear mechanism rather than calling later conflict inevitable.
  3. I can explain why U.S. Cold War and Iranian sovereignty frames could both persist.

Topic 3

CE - IR3 - The Ally Becomes the Enemy

Reverse History stop · 1979

Event title
CE - IR3 - The Ally Becomes the Enemy
Assignment to link
IR3 - Revolution and Hostages · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Trace how opposition to the Shah became a broad revolution, how the Islamic Republic emerged, and how the hostage crisis created a powerful American grievance alongside Iran's memory of 1953.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain how repression, rapid modernization, inequality, religion, and foreign influence combined in the revolution.
  2. I can distinguish the Iranian grievance associated with 1953 from the American grievance created in 1979.
  3. I can compare 1953 and 1979 using evidence and a causal mechanism.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can explain why several groups opposed the Shah without pretending they wanted the same future.
  2. I can use the opening-day hostage-crisis memorandum for what U.S. officials knew without treating it as proof of every participant's motive.
  3. I can use one specific fact from each turning point to defend which changed the relationship more.

Topic 4

CE - IR4 - Why Fight Far From Home?

Reverse History stop · 1980–1988

Event title
CE - IR4 - Why Fight Far From Home?
Assignment to link
IR4 - Security Strategy · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Use the Iran-Iraq War to investigate why invasion, isolation, the IRGC, missiles, and relationships with armed groups became central to Iranian security strategy.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain how the Iran-Iraq War shaped later security choices without treating it as the only cause.
  2. I can distinguish deterrence, asymmetric strategy, and power projection.
  3. I can explain why one strategy can look defensive to Iran and threatening to its neighbors.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can write the mechanism connecting invasion and isolation to later missiles or regional armed partnerships.
  2. I can use a specific wartime or institutional fact instead of relying on the label proxy.
  3. I can acknowledge evidence for both deterrence and power projection before weighing them.

Topic 5

CE - IR5 - The Nuclear Bargain

Reverse History thread · 1957–2018

Event title
CE - IR5 - The Nuclear Bargain
Assignment to link
IR5 - The Nuclear Bargain · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Follow Iran's nuclear program from U.S.-Iranian cooperation through the JCPOA, U.S. withdrawal, restored sanctions, reduced compliance, and the return of coercive pressure.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain what the JCPOA limited, what inspectors verified, and what the agreement left outside its scope.
  2. I can test the chain connecting U.S. withdrawal, sanctions, Iranian compliance, nuclear activity, and military pressure.
  3. I can compare the risks of maintaining an imperfect agreement with the risks of abandoning it.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can describe the bargain as nuclear restrictions and monitoring in exchange for nuclear-related sanctions relief.
  2. I can identify the strongest and weakest arrows in the post-2018 causal chain.
  3. I can argue whether the agreement's collapse made war more likely while acknowledging at least one other cause.

Topic 6

CE - IR6 - From Shadow War to Open War

Reverse History stop · 2023–2026

Event title
CE - IR6 - From Shadow War to Open War
Assignment to link
IR6 - Shadow War to Open War · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Trace how covert and indirect conflict crossed into direct state-to-state attacks in 2024, expanded into major war in 2025, and produced the intermittent 2026 conflict.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can distinguish a larger attack from an attack that changes what becomes thinkable next.
  2. I can explain how repeated retaliation can create path dependence without making war inevitable.
  3. I can compare deterrence-as-restraint with deterrence-as-an-escalation ladder.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can use one event from 2024 and one from 2025 or 2026 to identify a changed threshold.
  2. I can explain how one round altered the options or expectations in the next round.
  3. I can defend one turning point while addressing the strongest evidence for a different one.

Topic 7

CE - IR7 - The Hormuz Lever

Geography becomes power

Event title
CE - IR7 - The Hormuz Lever
Assignment to link
IR7 - The Hormuz Lever · 20 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Connect the Strait of Hormuz's chokepoint geography to the 1980s Tanker War, the measured collapse in 2026 oil flows, and the waterway's military, economic, and diplomatic uses.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can explain how a narrow waterway gives Iran leverage without requiring naval equality.
  2. I can use the change in estimated oil flows as evidence without claiming the numbers prove motive.
  3. I can identify a continuity and a difference between the Tanker War and the 2026 Hormuz crisis.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can complete the chain from narrow route to disrupted shipping to consequences beyond the Gulf.
  2. I can explain what the 21.6 to 4.9 million-barrel change establishes and what it cannot establish.
  3. I can decide whether Hormuz is primarily military, economic, or diplomatic leverage and support that ranking.

Topic 8

CE - IR8 - When Did This War Really Begin?

Causation synthesis

Event title
CE - IR8 - When Did This War Really Begin?
Assignment to link
IR8 - Final Causation Argument · 30 points
What it will look like in Canvas

OVERVIEW

Rebuild the entire causal chain, rank the most important turning points, test the strongest competing explanation, and write a final answer to the unit question.

LEARNING TARGETS
  1. I can connect evidence from several points in the chain through explicit causal mechanisms.
  2. I can state the strongest case for a turning point I did not rank first.
  3. I can distinguish the literal beginning of war from the explanatory beginning I defend.

SUCCESS CRITERIA
  1. I can use at least three specific pieces of evidence from different points in the chain.
  2. I can explain why a competing turning point matters before showing why mine carries more weight.
  3. I can name an explanatory beginning, define what it explains, and connect each piece of evidence to the final claim.
